# Introduction

<!--In this section you explain what you are trying to show.  Where did the data come from?  What is the research or other question you are trying to answer?.  If you skimp in this section expect to be marked down in your grade. Paint a picture of the project a couple of paragraphs is expected!-->

Data from triUmp. Question is: Is this drug effective in preventing aides on females specifically?

$H_0$ : No, drug is not effective at preventing aides in females.

$H_A$ : YES, drug is effective at preventing aides in females.

(A new  preventative aides drug (triUmpsal) is under test in clinical trials. Consider only the females, does this drug seem effective?  Hint - use dplyr to obtain that subpopulation with the filter command.)

```{r}
femaleData <- triUmp %>%
  filter(gender == "F")

names(femaleData)

table(femaleData$treatment)
```

## Descriptive Results

### Graphical Descriptive Results

<!--Graphical results here.  Make sure to show your code.  Provide appropriate labels for axes, giving units if possible, and provide a good title for the graph, too.  Use the graphical results to describe the patterns if any that exist in the data as focused toward the research question.
```{r}
barchartGC(~treatment + infected,data=femaleData)
barchartGC(~treatment + infected,data=femaleData, type="percent")

```  

This graph suggests that females who have taken the drug have a slightly higher percentage of getting aides. By filtering out males from the data, we have ensured that this is only data from female participants in the study, and checking the study *without* the filtering shows that the results are different then; essentially this just confirms the filtering was actually done right.

### Numerical Descriptive Results

```{r}
table1 <- xtabs(~treatment + infected, data=femaleData)
rowPerc(table1)
colPerc(table1)
```

According to the descriptive results, which have been once again filtered to only show females within the data, out of 100 female participants infected with aids roughly 59% of them had taken the drug, and 41% of them had taken the placebo, meaning there is a slightly higher amount of participants who have taken the drug and also have aids. Oh noes!!!

# Discussion and Conclusion

Data from triUmp. Original question is: Is this drug effective in preventing aides on females specifically?

We reject the null hypothesis and conclude that there is some relationship between the treatment drug and females infected with aides. More specifically, that females who have taken the drug have a slightly lower chance of being infected. The graphical summary and numerical results show that there are slightly fewer individuals out of a hundred who have taken the drug are infected, when compared to individuals that havent taken the drug and are infected. Because there are statistically more females than males in the study, we can infer that the results are still accurate when only focusing on females.
